assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a genuine invention in the sense of the Nobel statute: a bandgap-engineered unipolar intersubband laser, conceived from heterostructure design rather than from a material's natural gap, that opened mid-infrared and terahertz coherent sources. It is original, clear and has had lasting impact in spectroscopy, sensing and communications. From a materials-physics view it rests on atomically controlled epitaxial interfaces, which I value.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs was by a team; Faist and Capasso are the clear intellectual leaders. Cho is credited for the molecular-beam-epitaxy growth that made the layered structures possible, which supports a fair three-person configuration, though other Bell Labs co-authors (not in the supplied credit) complicate the picture.
assessment.maturity: Demonstrated over thirty years ago and independently reproduced and commercialised worldwide; the interpretation is stable and recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the epitaxial-growth contribution is to be weighed equally with the design concept.
Other early co-inventors exist outside the supplied credited names; I rely on my own recollection of the original author list and have not verified it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect established a new class of electronic phases with protected edge and surface states and reshaped the study of quantum materials. The theoretical proposal and the experimental HgTe demonstration form a coherent discovery with large lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal for the quantum spin Hall state; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental observation in HgTe wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The supplied names omit other theorists (for example those behind the HgTe prediction and the three-dimensional case), so a three-person prize leaves unresolved allocation.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups in transport and in angle-resolved photoemission and scanning microscopy of surfaces; the field is mature and the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: The theory credit for HgTe and for three-dimensional topological insulators lies outside the supplied names.
The compound nature (theory plus experiment plus 3D materials) may require different recognition for its parts.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal for quantum computation with trapped ions and its experimental realisation as high-fidelity gates and entangling operations is a foundational platform for quantum information processing and is of high lasting importance.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 theoretical proposal; Blatt's group led experimental realisation including entangling gates and quantum simulation. Wineland's contribution to ion control was already recognised in 2012, and others (for example Monroe, Wineland group gates) are not in the supplied credit, so the division of credit is partly unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple independent laboratories; commercial and research machines exist. Recognition is timely, with the risk that it overlaps with the 2012 prize rationale.
uncertainties: Overlap in scope with the 2012 prize for ion control.
Several experimental contributors are not in the supplied credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength lattice idea, improved the precision of timekeeping by orders of magnitude and enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. This is a clear invention with a defined and measurable result.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early clocks; Ye drove the record accuracy and many-body clock advances. Both are credited, which gives a clean two-person configuration; the role of other strontium and ytterbium groups is left out.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across several laboratories and sustained improvement in stability and accuracy; a redefinition of the second is under discussion, which suggests the field is mature though not yet formally settled.
uncertainties: Whether the prize would be seen as overlapping with earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock recognition.
The relative weighting of other independent clock groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, particularly with crystalline MgO barriers, underlies modern read heads and magnetic random-access memory. It is a materials and interface effect, whose strength depends on atomically controlled crystalline interfaces, and its practical impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: Room-temperature tunnelling magnetoresistance was reported in 1995 (Miyazaki's group, and Moodera's group, who is not in the supplied credit); the MgO coherent-tunnelling breakthrough was reported independently by Yuasa and by Parkin in 2004, supported by Butler's theory. With four names supplied and Moodera absent, attribution is difficult and I propose three.
assessment.maturity: Technologically mature and independently confirmed; the interpretation in terms of symmetry-filtered tunnelling is well established. The 2007 prize for giant magnetoresistance partly overlaps in subject.
uncertainties: Credit among Miyazaki, Moodera, Yuasa, Parkin and Butler is genuinely contested.
Possible perception of overlap with the 2007 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics realised strong light-matter coupling on a chip and is the basis for superconducting-qubit readout and control, with major impact on quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues made the theoretical proposal; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. The three-person configuration is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Highly confirmed. The recent 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits (as I recall it, not verified here) may make the timing of a closely related prize questionable.
uncertainties: Proximity to a recent superconducting-circuit prize that I have not verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the Mott-insulator transition and single-site quantum gas microscopy, gives controllable realisations of many-body models and is of lasting importance.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and collaborators proposed the Hubbard-model realisation; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch carried out the superfluid to Mott experiment; Greiner and Bloch developed quantum gas microscopes. The supplied names overlap with trapped-ion candidates, and the allocation across several strands is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced by many groups; quantum simulation results are still broadening.
uncertainties: Several experimental strands and groups are not in the supplied names.
Overlap with the Bose-Einstein condensation prize of 2001.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of magnetic skyrmion lattices and their real-space imaging established topologically protected spin textures with interesting transport and potential memory applications. It is of particular interest to me as a microscopist because real-space electron microscopy (Lorentz) and spin-polarised scanning probe imaging were decisive.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group reported the skyrmion lattice in MnSi by neutron scattering (2009); Tokura's group imaged it in real space with Lorentz microscopy (2010); Wiesendanger's group demonstrated atomic-scale skyrmions at surfaces. Theoretical predecessors (Bogdanov and others) are not in the supplied credit. I note my own field proximity as a possible bias.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in several materials, but the application track is still developing and the long-term importance, relative to other topological candidates, is less settled; possibly premature.
uncertainties: Theoretical precursor credit is absent from the supplied names.
